description: just a few guys conquering space
summary:
FireTrace turns 26 years of NASA fire detections over Brazil into a single burning-activity calendar that can honestly be compared across time - the core problem the challenge poses, because a rise in "hot spots" is often a change of satellite, not a change in fire.
We built a web application with a 3D globe and a year x month calendar over the full FIRMS archive for Brazil (29.2 million detections, Nov 2000 - Nov 2026). Users draw or type an area, pick dates, day/night, and the sensor view - MODIS, VIIRS, or harmonized - then compare the current month against the historical reference and export CSV.
Underneath is a measurement pipeline, not a multiplier. We rebuilt MODIS Aqua and VIIRS S-NPP fire detections from native Level-2 granules with their own geolocation and validity masks, kept only cell-periods where both sensors genuinely observed the same ground (579 valid pairs across ten months, 2012-2016), and fitted VIIRS-to-Aqua conversion separately for day and night and by season.
We ship the uncertainty too: coverage, refusal to compare when data are insufficient, and calibration status shown next to every number.
details:
What it does. 

FireTrace answers three questions for any area in Brazil: when is the fire season, which years burned more,and is the current month unusual. The landing screen offers Historical (Nov 2000 to today) or Projected (today to the same day next year). The globe shows an activity heatmap with 3D bars and clusters; a timeline plays the selected range at day/week/month/year steps; a calendar gives the year x month grid, seasonal profile and annual ranking; a card compares the running month against the historical reference on equal portions of the month. Area selection is a drawn rectangle, a country, a lat/lon cell or explicit W/S/E/N. Everything on screen exports to CSV with cell bounds, country,sensor and coverage. A retrospective case page reconstructs the Pantanal 2020 season - monthly heatmap, MODIS/VIIRS switch, Aqua/Terra calendars, per-platform mean FRP, and an hour-by-hour slider over 11 September.

How the harmonization works.

 The naive approach - multiply VIIRS counts by a constant - fails, because the two sensors differ in pixel size (375 m vs 1 km), overpass time and detection limit, and because a difference in coverage looks exactly like a difference in fire. So we went to the source: NASA Level-2 granules (MYD14/MYD03/MYD021KM for Aqua; VNP14IMG/VNP03IMG/VNP02IMG for S-NPP), 2,695 granules and ~159 GB, re-gridded to 0.01 deg cells on local solar days with each sensor's native geolocation and validity mask preserved. A cell-period becomes a valid pair only when both sensors confirmably observed it - that gate alone discarded 53% of candidate periods (579 valid pairs from 1,220). Conversion is fitted on that common support, separately for day and night and by season, with observed zeros retained. Outage days are dropped in pairs so an instrument failure never becomes a fire signal. Strata without positive VIIRS mass stay UNCALIBRATED rather than being filled with a plausible number.

Validation. 

The protocol and thresholds were frozen in git before fitting; predictions were hashed before evaluation labels were attached. Candidates were compared on identical support with monthly WAPE: the ratio estimator M1 reached 9.00% (Novo Progresso, day) and 15.83% (Apui, day), and a gradient-boosting challenger lost in every aggregate cross-section - so the simpler estimator shipped. Six regions have been evaluated; the national verdict is still INCONCLUSIVE,and the app says so. The seasonal projection beats previous-year persistence by 25.29% at night and loses by 4.76% in daytime. Those numbers are in the UI and in the docs exactly as measured, including the ones that disappoint us.

Benefits and impact. 

Fire teams, land managers and researchers currently cannot tell whether this August is worse than usual, because the instrument changed mid-record. A comparable series makes anomaly detection, seasonal staffing and long-term trend work possible on the same footing. The method is reusable: the gate is "did both sensors see it", not anything Brazil-specific.

Tools. 

Python 3.12 (standard library for the baseline estimators; NumPy, statsmodels, h5py for L2 decoding and the FRP model; ecCodes for GRIB forecasts) with hash-locked dependencies. Frontend: JavaScript + Vite, MapLibre GL JS for the globe, Three.js for the starfield and 3D bars, a Web Worker for aggregation, and a generated design-token stylesheet.Data: NASA FIRMS API, NASA Earthdata CMR + LP DAAC/LAADS DAAC for L2 granules, NASA POWER for hourly weather history, NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery, SRTMGL1 elevation, NOAA GFS forecasts and GOES-19 ABI. The whole pipeline runs on a laptop with no cloud dependency; the web build deploys as static files.

Creativity. 

Three things we did differently. First, we treated the challenge as a measurement problem and rebuilt detections from native granules rather than scaling the convenient summary product - the honest answer needed the hard path. Second, the interface makes the problem visible instead of hiding it: you switch MODIS to VIIRS to harmonized on the same area and watch the artifact appear and then disappear. Third, we made refusal a first-class feature - when a month lacks a comparable reference, the app removes the comparison column and explains why, rather than printing a number that looks fine.

What we considered.

 We deliberately scoped to Brazil (confirmed acceptable by the challenge navigators) rather than claiming a global calibration we could not validate in 25 hours, and documented every exclusion on the methodology page. We handled the S-NPP data stop of 2 November 2026 by bridging to NOAA-20 explicitly rather than letting the series end silently. We used colourblind-safe palettes (YlOrRd for counts, PuOr for anomalies), keyboard navigation and a table view of every chart. And we set first-hour and checkpoint gates with pre-declared responses to failure, so that under deadline pressure the decision to stop was already made before we were tempted not to.
